I have farmed this 1.1 mu plot in Quzhou County for 30 years. I know our soil and weather like the back of my hand. With only three people in my household and some of us working off-farm, I cannot afford risky experiments or backbreaking labor. I stick to the wheat-maize rotation because it is the only system that fits our land and our calendar.

For wheat, I will sow improved seeds in mid-October after preparing the field with rotary tillage. I will apply about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu—half as base fertilizer and half topdressed at green-up—plus phosphate and potash. I will irrigate three times: the overwintering water, the jointing water, and one during grain filling if the rain does not come. I will spray herbicide once after sowing, and if I see aphids or rust, I will spray one more time.

For maize, after we harvest wheat in early June, the window is tight. I will sow hybrid maize seeds right away with no-tillage—just clear the stubble and plant—to save time and fuel since my family has limited labor. I will apply similar nitrogen rates and irrigate twice, at the big trumpet stage and during grain filling, plus a sowing irrigation if the soil is dry. Two pesticide applications will be enough: one herbicide and one for corn borers if they appear.

I do not chase record yields. I farm steadily. If the weather is fair, I expect about 520 kg per mu from wheat and 560 kg per mu from maize, which is decent for our area.
